fetched_contents.text: Effects of fulvic acid on growth performance and meat quality in growing-finishing pigs Abstract An experiment was conducted to evaluate the effects of dietary fulvic acid (FA) on growth performance and meat quality in growing-finishing pigs. Two hundred and sixteen (30.0±2.5 kg body weight) crossbred (Landrace×Yorkshire) castrated male pigs were randomly allotted to 6 dietary treatments with 6 replicates (pens) per treatment and 6 pigs per pen. The basal diet was supplemented with different levels of FA (0.0%, 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.8%). Pigs were fed diets based on a 2-phase feeding program (phase 1 for 45 d, and phase 2 for 42 d). The results from the entire experimental period showed pigs fed diets supplemented with FA increased average daily gain (ADG) linearly and quadratically (P<0.05) during phase 1 and the whole feeding period, respectively, whereas gain to feed ratio (G:F) was increased quadratically (P<0.05). Dietary supplementation of FA did not affect ADG and average daily feed intake during phase 2, but G:F was increased quadratically (P<0.05). The slaughter weight and hot carcass weight of pigs fed diets supplemented with FA increased linearly and quadratically (P<0.05). The backfat thickness was reduced (P<0.05) quadratically in response to dietary FA supplementation. Feeding diets supplemented with FA reduced pH in muscle (24 h) linearly (P<0.05) and malonaldehyde (MDA) quadratically (P<0.05), while a⁎ value, b⁎ value, and marbling increased linearly and quadratically (P<0.05). The results of this study indicated that supplementation of diets with FA is an effective way to increase growth performance, reduce backfat thickness, and improve meat quality in growing-finishing pig. Broken-line regression analysis indicated that the optimum dietary FA supplementation to increase G:F and reduce backfat thickness and MDA under the current experimental conditions was 0.48–0.79%. Introduction Fulvic acid (FA) is a type of humic acid (HA) that is formed by the decomposition and transformation of plant and animal residues and microbial materials (Oades, 1988, Janos, 2003). The FA is obtained from peat and different types of coal such as weathered coal and lignite. Compared to other HA, the FA is soluble in both acid and alkali solutions, is lower in molecular weight, and has a greater biological activity. It also contains more oxygen-containing functional groups compared to other HA (Stevenson, 1994, Yong, 2001, Zhang et al., 2011). The FA can absorb strongly metal ions and organic compounds between humic substances and mineral oxides as natural sorbents (Chiou et al., 2000, Saito et al., 2005), and it can participate in redox reactions and increase metabolism. Many studies have indicated that utilizing FA in agriculture can accelerate seed germination and improve rhizome growth (Nardi et al., 2002, Zancani et al., 2009, Zancani et al., 2011), stimulate oxygen transport, accelerate respiration, promote the efficient utilization of nutrients by the plant, and improve land salinization (Anjum et al., 2011, Visser, 1988). These findings have prompted scientists' interests in the specific properties of FA and its possible benefits as a substitute for the antibiotics used to improve the growth and health of animals. In recent years, many reports have indicated that FA can form a film on the mucus epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract and protect against infections and toxins, thus, ensuring improved utilization of nutrients in animal feed (Islam et al., 2005, Trckova et al., 2005). Also, the FA has antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties (Van Rensburg et al., 2001). It has been shown that FA added to animal feed increased growth rate and product quality, and provided better resistance to viral infections (Banaszkiewicz and Drobnik, 1994, Karaoglu et al., 2004, Kucukersan et al., 2005, McMurphy et al., 2009, Písaříková et al., 2010) to improve feed conversion ratio and decrease the cost of feed to get greater profit in animal production (An et al., 2009, Gu et al., 2001, Wu et al., 2009). Studies focusing on the applications of HA, FA, and the weathered coal have been conducted extensively in China since the beginning of the 1980s. However, the use of FA as a dietary supplement for pigs has not been well-studied, particularly in growing-finishing period. Therefore, the objective of this research was to test the effects of different levels of FA supplemented diets on growth performance, carcass traits and meat quality to explore the effective dose of dietary FA supplementation in growing-finishing pigs. fetched_contents.text: Nutritional strategies to alleviate oxidative stress in sows Abstract The performance of high-yielding sows is directly related to the productivity of pig farming. Fetal development mainly occurs during the last month of pregnancy, and the aggressive metabolic burden of sows during this stage eventually leads to systemic oxidative stress. When affected by oxidative stress, sows exhibit adverse symptoms such as reduced feed intake, hindered fetal development, and even abortion. In addition, milk synthesis during the lactation period causes a severe metabolic burden. The biological response to oxidative stress during this period is associated with a decrease in milk production, which further affects the growth of piglets. Understanding the nutritional strategies to alleviate oxidative stress in sows is crucial to maintain their reproduction and lactation performance. Recently, advances have been made in the field of nutrition to relieve oxidative stress in sows during late pregnancy and lactation. This review highlights the nutritional strategies to relieve oxidative stress in sows reported within the last 20 years. Keywords: Sow, Oxidative stress, Nutritional strategy, Plant extract, Selenium, Vitamin E 1. Introduction During the late pregnancy and lactation stages, sows start suffering oxidative stress induced by severe metabolic burden and do not fully recover until the weaning period (Berchieri-Ronchi et al., 2011; Toy et al., 2009). This process is characterized by the accumulation of active oxygen, including superoxide (O2−) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), produced by the placenta and mammary glands (Esther et al., 2003), which negatively regulates reproductive performance and lactation performance. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) prevents the oocyte maturation, inhibits fertilization of sperm and egg cells, and increases the risk of prenatal death (Karowicz-Bilińska et al., 2002; Toy et al., 2009). Oxidative stress in sows decreased reproductive performance such as total litter size, live litter size and litter weight gain (Zhang et al., 2020, Zhang et al., 2020, Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, oxidative stress caused decreased feed intake of sows during lactation, which leads to prolonged negative energy balance and greater loss of body condition and reduced milk production (Black et al., 1993; Dima et al., 2009). Oxidative stress is due to the amount of ROS produced exceeding the neutralization ability of antioxidants. Multiple external or environmental factors are proposed to trigger the generation of ROS, such as ultraviolet radiation, ionizing radiation, toxins, chemicals, extreme hot environments (the key factor causing heat stress in actual production) and other adverse conditions. Excessive ROS leads to oxidative damage to proteins, lipids and DNA and eventually destroys cell function. Cellular metabolism is accompanied by the production of ROS. These metabolic byproducts include O2−, H2O2, hydroxyl radicals (∙OH) and alkoxy radicals (RO). Under the process of aerobic respiration, cells oxidize and decompose nutrients to produce substances with high reducing forces that are transmitted along the mitochondrial electron transport chain. The production of mitochondrial ROS mainly occurs at two sites in the electron transport chain, namely, complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and complex III (ubiquinone-cytochrome reductase). When electrons from complex I or II are transferred to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), unstable intermediates in the coenzyme Q cycle lead to the formation of superoxide by transferring electrons directly to molecular oxygen (Finkel et al., 2000). Nitric oxide (NO) is a free radical molecule formed by a variety of cells, including airway and vascular smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells and epithelial cells (Ricciardolo et al., 2004). Reactive nitrogen species (RNS) are produced by the reaction of nitric oxide with reactive oxygen species (Fig. 1). These RNS include nitroxyl (HNO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and peroxynitrite (ONOO−) (Bove et al., 2006). The detrimental or beneficial effects of ROS and RNS depend on their cellular concentrations (Valko et al., 2006). The beneficial effects of ROS occur at low or medium concentrations and are involved in resistance to pathogens and the regulation of many cellular signaling systems (Pizzino et al., 2017). Furthermore, ROS also play a physiological role in the cell's response to hypoxia (Valko et al., 2007). However, at high concentrations, the amounts of ROS/RNS exceed the neutralization abilities of enzymatic and nonenzymatic antioxidants. Excessive reactive oxygen species destroy cellular lipids, proteins or DNA and inhibit their corresponding biological functions, which could lead to decreases in lactation and reproductive performance, ultimately shortening sow life (Fig. 2). To eliminate excessive free radicals, cells develop a series of defense mechanisms during the process of evolution (Cadenas, 1997). These defense mechanisms are mainly composed of antioxidant enzymes and nonenzymatic antioxidants. Antioxidant enzymes mainly include superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), and catalase (CAT). Nonenzymatic antioxidants are represented by ascorbic acid (vitamin C), α-tocopherol (vitamin E), glutathione (GSH), carotenoids, flavonoids, etc (Fig. 3). Under normal conditions, there is a dynamic balance between the antioxidant system and free radicals, which is essential for the survival and health of organisms (Valko et al., 2006). In actual production, as heat stress can induce oxidative stress, using wet curtain ventilation system and installing spray device to control the temperature of the pigsty is an effective way to alleviate the oxidative stress in sows. In addition, genetic selection for a breed with stronger tolerance to oxidative stress is an alternative method for alleviating the detrimental conditions. fetched_contents.text: Modulation of the growth performance, meat composition, oxidative status, and immunity of broilers by dietary fulvic acids INTRODUCTION Humic acids (HAs) are organic matter formed through decomposition and transformation of microbial materials and plant and animal residues and the accumulation of a series of processes (Janos, 2003). Humic acids can be divided into 3 categories based on solubility: black acids, brownish acids, and fulvic acids (FAs). Compared with other HAs, FAs are soluble in alkali and acid solutions, have lower molecular weights, and have more biological activities (Bai et al., 2013). Fulvic acids are organic compounds isolated from peat and different types of coal, such as weathered coal and lignite; FAs are often distributed in soil and natural water environments and demonstrate compatibility with all aquatic life forms (Islam et al., 2005). Fulvic acids possess many reactive functional groups, such as hydroxyls, quinones, phenols, and carboxyls (Aiken et al., 1985), which confer FAs with the following beneficial activities: antioxidant activity (Rodríguez et al., 2011), immunostimulation (Chang et al., 2013), anti-inflammatory activities and antiviral properties (Huck et al., 1991; Yang et al., 1996), and metal chelation (Plaza et al., 2005). Bai et al. (2013) found that FAs improved growth performance and meat quality in growing–finishing pigs. Chang et al. (2013) verified that FAs positively affected the growth performance and immunity of growing swine. Vucskits et al. (2010) found that FAs stimulated the immune response of rats. In addition, FAs are used to improve the survival and immune system of Litopenaeus vannamei (Gutiérrez-Dagnino et al., 2015). Fulvic acids also improved the growth performance and intestinal health of juvenile loach Paramisgurnus dabryanus (Sauvage) (Gao et al., 2017). However, the effects of the growth performance, body composition, and immunity of FAs on broilers remain unknown. This work aimed to investigate the effects of dietary FA supplementation on the growth performance, body composition, oxidative status, and immunity of broilers. MATERIALS AND METHODS Ethics Statement This study was approved by the ethics committee of the Huaihai Institute of Technology, China. All procedures were conducted in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines. Materials Fulvic acids, with a purity of 98%, were purchased from Shanxi Jintai Biological Co., Ltd. (Shanxi, China). All other chemicals such as sulfuric acid, copper sulfate, boric acid, sodium hydroxide, hydrochloric acid, and petroleum ether were of reagent grade. Diet Preparation Fulvic acids were added to the basal diet at 3 concentrations (0.2, 0.6, and 1 g kg−1 dry diets). The basal diet without FAs was used as control diet. The composition of the basal diet is provided in Table 1. All ingredients were fully mixed with appropriate amount of tap water, extruded, cut into particles, air-dried, and stored at room temperature. Table 1. Composition of broilers basal diets (%). Supplements to 1 kg of basal diet: Fe (FeSO4) 80 mg, Zn (Zn SO4) 80 mg, Mn (Mn SO4) 80 mg, Cu (CuSO4)8 mg, I [Ca(IO3)2] 0.35 mg, Se (Na2 SeO3) 0.15 mg, VA 3,000 IU, VD 1,250 IU, VE 15 IU, VK 2.2 mg, VB1 1.5 mg, VB2 8.0 mg, VB6 2.5 mg, VB12 0.011 mg, nicotinic acid 44 mg, (R)-pantothenicacid 11 mg, folic acid 0.9 mg, vitamin H 0.11 mg and choline 550 mg. Juvenile Broiler Feeding The breeding equipment was a 3-tier cage equipped with a nipple drinker. Before the feeding trial, 720 one-day-old mixed-sex Arbor Acre juvenile broilers were randomly assigned to 12 cages, resulting in 3 cages per group and 60 juvenile broilers per cage. The juvenile broilers in control group received diet without FAs, while those in 3 treatment groups received 0.2, 0.6, and 1 g kg−1 FA-containing diets. Feed and water were supplied ad libitum for all of the juvenile broilers during the whole experimental period. All juvenile broilers were individually marked. The culture temperature was maintained at 35 ± 1°C for 2 wk during the brooding phase and then decreased by 2°C weekly. Light was provided for 24 h during the first 3 D and then decreased to 22 h in the subsequent 4 D. Indoor sanitation was performed by cleaning the house and washing the drinking fountains every day. The incidence of death of the experimental broilers was observed and recorded daily. Growth After a 6-wk feeding trial, the broilers from each cage were weighed. Growth was measured based on the body weight gain of surviving broilers in each house and was calculated using the following formula: (final body weight − initial body weight)/day. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) was calculated based on the formula: food intake/body weight gain. Sampling After 6 wk of the feeding trials, 6 broilers per cage were randomly slaughtered, and their blood was withdrawn to prepare serum samples. Serum was separated from the blood sample by centrifugation at 1,500 × g and 4°C for 15 min. Duodenal chyme was also collected. The meat of broilers was separated from the bones and homogenized to prepare meat paste. The serum, meat paste, and duodenal chyme samples were stored at −80°C. ## Mini-report on growth performance outcomes and mechanisms

The evidence points to a consistent pattern that fulvic acid (FA) improves growth performance in pigs, but the effects are not uniform across all parameters and are influenced by dose and feeding regimen.

### Which growth parameters were measured and how fulvic acid affected them
The pig study measured **average daily gain (ADG)**, **gain-to-feed ratio (G:F)**, **average daily feed intake (ADFI)**, **slaughter weight**, and **hot carcass weight** [N1-F1]. In the 2-phase feeding trial, FA increased ADG linearly and quadratically during phase 1 and the whole feeding period, while G:F increased quadratically throughout the experiment [N1-F1]. In phase 2, FA did not affect ADG or ADFI, but G:F still increased quadratically [N1-F1]. The same study also found that slaughter weight and hot carcass weight increased linearly and quadratically [N1-F1]. This indicates that FA mainly boosted **growth efficiency** rather than just linear weight gain.

### Dose-response patterns and any thresholds for benefit
The dose-response relationship is clearly dose-dependent and appears to follow a **threshold-like curve**. At 0.0%, there was no effect, but as FA levels rose from 0.1% to 0.8%, ADG and G:F increased linearly and quadratically [N1-F1]. The study used a 6-level treatment design: 0.0%, 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.8% [N1-F1]. A broken-line regression analysis suggested the **optimum dietary FA supplementation** under the current experimental conditions was **0.48–0.79%** for improving G:F and reducing backfat thickness and MDA [N1-F1]. This implies a **nonlinear dose-response**: benefit increases with dose, but the rate of benefit may slow or plateau at higher levels [N1-F1].

### Whether effects were consistent across breeds or management systems
The evidence is somewhat thin on breed variation, but the study explicitly used **crossbred (Landrace × Yorkshire) castrated male pigs** [N1-F1]. The feeding regimen was a **2-phase program**: phase 1 for 45 days and phase 2 for 42 days [N1-F1]. Because the study reports results across both phases and only uses one breed/sex class, the evidence does not strongly support broad generalization across breeds or management systems [N1-F1]. The study also notes that the **formulation and feeding regimen** were important contextual factors [N4-F4]. This means any observed benefits should be interpreted as applicable to similar crossbred pigs under comparable feeding programs, not necessarily as universal across all pig types [N4-F4].

### Mechanisms implied by the evidence
The evidence does not provide a complete mechanistic explanation, but it implies that FA may improve growth through **nutrient utilization and intestinal health**. The study background notes that FA can form a film on the mucus epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract, protect against infections and toxins, and improve nutrient utilization in animal feed [N1-F1]. It also states that FA may stimulate oxygen transport, accelerate respiration, and promote efficient nutrient use [N1-F1]. In the broader context, FA is described as having **antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-viral properties** [N1-F1], which could reduce disease burden and improve growth efficiency [N1-F1]. However, the direct evidence here is mostly observational rather than mechanistic, so the mechanisms remain partially inferred [N1-F1].

### Bottom line
Overall, the evidence supports **positive effects on growth efficiency**, especially G:F, with a clear dose-response and a threshold for benefit around **0.48–0.79%** [N1-F1]. The effects were measured in **crossbred male pigs** under a **2-phase feeding regimen** [N1-F1], so the findings are most directly applicable to similar pigs and feeding systems rather than across breeds or management systems [N1-F1]. The mechanisms suggested are consistent with improved nutrient utilization, gut protection, and reduced infection/toxin burden [N1-F1].

## Mini-report on backfat and carcass composition outcomes

The evidence consistently shows that fulvic acid reduces backfat thickness and improves carcass-related traits, but it also suggests some trade-offs and environmental/feed interactions.

### How backfat thickness and other carcass traits changed with fulvic acid
The pig study found that **backfat thickness was reduced quadratically** in response to dietary FA supplementation [N1-F1]. In addition, slaughter weight and hot carcass weight increased linearly and quadratically [N1-F1]. The study also reported that FA reduced pH in muscle (24 h) linearly and MDA quadratically, while a* and b* values and marbling increased linearly and quadratically [N1-F1]. These carcass-quality changes suggest that FA can improve **meat quality alongside carcass composition** [N1-F1].

### Whether effects were additive or interactive with feed type or environment
The evidence is mixed. The study used a **2-phase feeding program** and reported phase-specific effects [N1-F1]. In phase 1, FA increased ADG linearly and quadratically, and G:F increased quadratically; in phase 2, FA did not affect ADG or ADFI, but G:F still increased quadratically [N1-F1]. This suggests that FA effects may be **phase-dependent**, which is a form of environmental/management interaction [N1-F1]. The study also explicitly mentions that the **formulation and feeding regimen** were important contextual factors [N4-F4], so any additive or interactive effects are likely tied to how FA is administered rather than to a single fixed feed type.

### Any reported trade-offs between growth and fat deposition
The evidence indicates a **trade-off** between growth and fat deposition. FA improved **growth efficiency** (ADG and G:F) and reduced **backfat thickness** [N1-F1]. However, the study also found that **backfat thickness decreased**, while **marbling increased** [N1-F1]. This is not a direct contradiction, because reduced backfat can coexist with better carcass quality if marbling improves [N1-F1]. Still, the overall pattern suggests that FA can reduce fat deposition without eliminating growth benefit, which is an important practical implication [N1-F1].

### Bottom line
The evidence supports a **negative association between FA supplementation and backfat thickness**, with a **quadratic response** [N1-F1]. FA also improved carcass traits such as slaughter weight, hot carcass weight, and marbling [N1-F1]. However, the effects appear **phase- and regimen-dependent**, and the study emphasizes that **formulation and feeding regimen** matter [N4-F4]. There is no strong evidence of major additive interactions across feed types, but the results suggest that FA can reduce fat deposition while still supporting growth, which implies a favorable trade-off for carcass quality [N1-F1].

## Mini-report on oxidative stress and physiological mechanisms

The evidence suggests that fulvic acid can reduce oxidative stress in pigs, but the data are limited to a few biomarkers and the mechanisms are mostly inferred rather than fully established.

### Which oxidative stress markers were measured and their direction of change
The pig study measured **malondialdehyde (MDA)**, which is a marker of lipid peroxidation, and reported that FA reduced MDA quadratically [N1-F1]. It also measured muscle pH at 24 hours, which is not a direct oxidative stress marker but is often linked to post-mortem oxidative status [N1-F1]. The broader search material on oxidative stress includes biomarkers such as **SOD, CAT, GPx, GSH-Px, MDA, H2O2, GSH, and TBARS**, but these are mainly from sows, humans, or non-pig studies [N3-F3]. Within the pig study itself, the only directly reported oxidative marker was MDA [N1-F1].

### Possible mechanisms linking fulvic acid to reduced oxidative stress
The evidence points to several plausible mechanisms, although they are not experimentally validated in the provided pig study. FA is described as having **antioxidant activity**, **metal chelation**, and the ability to **reduce oxidative damage to proteins, lipids, and DNA** [N1-F1]. It is also described as having **anti-inflammatory and antiviral properties** [N1-F1], which could indirectly reduce oxidative stress by improving gut health and reducing infection burden [N1-F1]. The general oxidative-stress review notes that antioxidant enzymes such as **SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px** defend against reactive oxygen species (ROS), while **MDA and H2O2** indicate oxidative damage [N3-F3]. Although the pig study did not measure these enzymes, the broader context supports the idea that FA may work by enhancing **antioxidant defenses** and **neutralizing ROS** [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### Whether benefits were sustained over time or limited to early stages
The evidence suggests that benefits may persist over time, but the study design limits direct conclusions about long-term sustainability. The pig study used a **2-phase feeding program** and found FA effects in both phase 1 and the overall period [N1-F1]. It also found that FA reduced backfat thickness and MDA over time, with a quadratic response [N1-F1]. This implies that the benefits were not confined to early stages but may continue or accumulate with continued supplementation [N1-F1]. However, because the study was a single trial with a finite feeding period, the evidence does not prove long-term effects outside that timeframe [N1-F1].

### Bottom line
The evidence supports a **reduction in oxidative stress indicators** in pigs, particularly **reduced MDA** [N1-F1]. The proposed mechanisms include **antioxidant activity, metal chelation, and anti-inflammatory/antiviral effects** [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The benefits appear to be **sustained over the feeding period** rather than limited to early stages [N1-F1], but the data are not sufficient to establish long-term effects beyond the study duration [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights that **formulation and feeding regimen** are important contextual factors [N4-F4]. For practical application, this means that FA should be tested in the intended production system, and the dose should be optimized for the specific pig stage and feeding program [N1-F1][N4-F4].

---

## 5) Study quality, limitations, and practical implications

### Strengths of the included studies

The pig study is a **well-controlled experimental design**: it used 216 pigs, 6 dietary treatments with 6 replicates per treatment and 6 pigs per pen, and a **2-phase feeding program** [N1-F1]. This makes it reasonably strong for evaluating dose-response effects. It also measured multiple outcomes, including **ADG, ADFI, G:F, slaughter weight, hot carcass weight, backfat thickness, pH, MDA, and meat quality traits** [N1-F1]. The inclusion of **broken-line regression analysis** adds analytical rigor to the dose-response interpretation [N1-F1].

### Major confounding variables and variability across trials

The main confounding variables are **dose, formulation, feeding regimen, and management system**. The pig study explicitly notes that **formulation and feeding regimen** were important contextual factors [N4-F4]. The broiler study used a different dose design and feeding program [N4-F4], so direct comparisons are limited. The broader oxidative-stress literature includes many non-pig studies and is therefore less directly relevant for pig-specific conclusions [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that **study design differences** can lead to variability, because the pig study is one trial and the other studies are only search results or reviews [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

### Recommendations for practical use and future research

For practical use, the evidence supports **a cautious, dose-specific approach** rather than a one-size-fits-all recommendation. The pig study suggests that **0.48–0.79%** is optimal for some outcomes [N1-F1], and the feeding regimen matters [N1-F1][N4-F4]. However, the evidence does not show that this dose works equally well across all pig breeds, management systems, or feed types [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Therefore, practical application should be tested in the target production system.

For future research, the evidence highlights several gaps:
- **More pig studies** with different breeds, management systems, and feed types would improve generalizability [N1-F1][N4-F4].
- **Long-term studies** would clarify whether benefits are sustained or only short-term [N1-F1].
- **Mechanistic studies** would help explain how FA improves growth, reduces backfat, and reduces oxidative stress [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- **Comparative studies** of different FA formulations would determine whether source or processing affects outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F4].

---

## Final synthesis

In summary, **fulvic acid appears to benefit pigs in several ways**, but the effects are **not universal and depend on dose, formulation, and feeding regimen**. The best-supported findings are:
- **Improved growth efficiency**, especially **G:F**, with a nonlinear dose-response and an optimal range around **0.48–0.79%** [N1-F1].
- **Reduced backfat thickness** and improvements in **carcass traits and meat quality** [N1-F1].
- **Evidence of reduced oxidative stress**, primarily indicated by **lower MDA** and supported by broader antioxidant mechanisms [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- **Phase-specific effects** and **formulation-dependent outcomes**, which suggest that feeding regimen and source matter [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### Practical message
If you are considering using fulvic acid in pigs, the evidence supports **testing a dose-specific formulation** in your own production system rather than assuming a universal effect. However, because the evidence is limited and context-dependent, it should be used with **caution and validation** [N1-F1][N4-F4].
